section.title: The Vine and the Branches
section.sectionRationale: The Upper Room Discourse continues with the last I am saying: I am the true vine. Jesus pictures the union of Himself and His people as a vine and its branches, from which alone fruit can come, and calls His disciples to remain in Him and in His love. He raises them from servants to friends, roots their fruitfulness in His choosing, and warns that a world which hated Him will hate them too, even as the Spirit and they together will testify to Him.
section.thesis: Jesus is the true vine and His people are the branches, so that fruitful life comes only by remaining in Him and in His love, keeping His command to love one another; He calls them friends and chose them to bear lasting fruit, warning that the world which hated Him will hate them, while the Spirit and they together bear witness to Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the true vine and the branches and the call to remain and bear fruit; the greater love and the raising of servants to friends chosen to bear lasting fruit; and the hatred of the world and the twin witness of the Spirit and the disciples.

units.label: I am the true vine
units.note: remain in Me and bear much fruit

verses.text: “{{egoeimi|I am}} the true {{ampelos|vine}}, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.
He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no {{karpos|fruit}}, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful.
You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.
{{meno|Remain}} in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me.
I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned.
If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.
This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples.
As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love.
If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love.
I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.
This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends.
You are My friends if you do what I command you.
No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you.
You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you.
This is My command to you: Love one another.

units.label: The hatred of the world
units.note: the Spirit and you will testify

verses.text: If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first.
If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.
Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘No servant is greater than his master.’ If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well.
But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me.
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin.
Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well.
If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father.
But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’
When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, He will testify about Me.
And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. The seventh and last of the great I am sayings, I am the true vine, completes the series. As with the others, the phrase names both a rich image and the divine self; Jesus is the true vine over against unfruitful Israel, the source from which all fruitful life in His people must flow.

ampelos.gloss: Vine. Israel was often pictured as God's vine or vineyard, frequently a fruitless and disappointing one. Jesus declares Himself the true vine, the faithful Israel who bears the fruit God sought, and the living stock into which His people are grafted so that they too may bear fruit that pleases the Father.

karpos.gloss: Fruit. The fruit the Father seeks is the life that flows from union with Christ: love, obedience, answered prayer, and the ingathering of others, fruit that lasts. It is not self-produced but the natural yield of a branch that remains in the vine, and its abundance brings glory to the Father and proves genuine discipleship.

meno.gloss: To remain, abide, stay. The key word of the chapter, used repeatedly: remain in Me, and I in you. Abiding is a settled, continuing union with Christ, kept by holding to His word and His love; apart from it a branch can do nothing but wither. To remain in Christ is the secret of all fruitfulness.

basic.context: Still in the upper room, Jesus gives His last I am saying: I am the true vine, and My Father is the gardener. His disciples are branches, and the one lesson pressed again and again is, remain in Me. A branch cut off from the vine can do nothing and withers; a branch that remains bears much fruit. Jesus calls them to remain in His love by keeping His commands, above all the command to love one another. He lifts them from servants to friends, reminds them He chose them to bear lasting fruit, and warns that the world that hated Him will hate them too, though the Spirit and they will testify to Him.
basic.hermeneutics: The vine imagery draws on the Old Testament picture of Israel as God's vine, often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine who succeeds where Israel failed. The key word is remain, or abide. The key questions are, where does fruitful life come from, and how do we stay connected to Christ. The answer is union with Him, kept by His word and His love. The warning about fruitless branches calls for self-examination, and the promise of friendship and lasting fruit gives deep assurance.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on a few words. Jesus is the true ampelos, the vine, the last ego eimi saying. His people are branches meant to bear karpos, fruit. And the repeated command is meno, remain, abide in Me and in My love, for apart from Him they can do nothing.
basic.typology: The vine fulfills the image of Israel as God's vineyard, now realized in the true vine, Christ, and His people grafted into Him. The friendship with God echoes Abraham, called the friend of God, now extended to all who obey Christ.
basic.christ: Christ is the true vine, the source of all fruitful life, whose love the branches must remain in. He lays down His life for His friends, the greatest love, and He chose His people to bear lasting fruit. The world's hatred of Him is passed on to His own.
basic.god: God the Father is the gardener who prunes for fruit and is glorified when His people bear much fruit. He loves the Son, and the Son's love for His people mirrors it. To hate the Son is to hate the Father.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5 and Psalm 80 picture Israel as God's vine. John 13 gave the command to love. Galatians 5 names the fruit of the Spirit. James 2 calls Abraham the friend of God.
basic.oneStory: Where Israel the vine failed to bear fruit, Jesus the true vine bears the fruit God sought and makes His people fruitful branches in Himself. Remaining in Him, loved and chosen as friends, they bear lasting fruit for the Father's glory, even as the hostile world rages, and the Spirit joins their witness to Christ.

context.literary:
John 15 has three clear movements, and each is announced by a change of image. In verses 1 to 11 the picture is organic: a vine, a gardener, branches, pruning, fruit, fire. In verses 12 to 17 the picture becomes personal: commands, friends, servants, choosing and appointing. In verses 18 to 27 it turns hostile: a world that hates, witnesses who are hated, and a Spirit who testifies. The movement runs from union with Christ, to love within the community, to opposition from outside it. John has laid out the Christian life from the inside to the edge.

The chapter is held together by repeating key words. 'Remain' appears more than ten times in verses 4 to 10, until the reader cannot miss it. 'Fruit' appears in verses 2, 4, 5, 8, 16, and 'love' in nearly every verse from 9 to 17. The effect is a spiral. Remaining produces fruit, fruit glorifies the Father, the Father's glory is the Son's joy, and the joy is the Son's love poured into His own. Each phrase explains the next, so the section reads like a single sentence stretched over eleven verses.

There is a quiet word play in verses 2 and 3. The Father 'prunes,' kathairei, every fruitful branch, and in the next breath Jesus says they are already 'clean,' katharoi. The two words come from the same root. The pruning of the Father and the cleansing of the word are one action seen from two sides. The link also returns to John 13:10, where Jesus told the disciples, 'you are clean,' so the vine discourse is the next step in the same night's teaching.

The final movement turns on a double witness. The Advocate will testify about Jesus, verse 26, and the disciples must testify as well, verse 27, because they have been with Him from the beginning. The chapter ends not with comfort but with a commission, which prepares for the sharper warnings of the next chapter.
context.historical:
The vine was one of the commonest sights in Israel. Vineyards covered the hill country, and the whole year of a vinedresser's work centred on keeping the vines healthy and productive. Growers cut back the vine hard because a vine left unpruned puts its strength into leaves and wood, not into grapes. Dead or fruitless wood could not be used for building or furniture, a point Ezekiel makes bitterly, 'Can wood be taken from it to make something useful?' Ezekiel 15:3, and it was gathered and burned. The audience would have grasped every detail of the image without explanation.

The vine was also the nation's emblem. According to Josephus and the Mishnah, a large golden vine decorated the entrance of the temple in Jerusalem, and vine clusters appeared on Jewish coinage in the first and second revolts against Rome. When Jesus says 'I am the true vine' in a city that wore the vine as its badge, He is making a claim about who now embodies the people of God. The word 'true' hints that the earlier vine had not borne the fruit God sought.

Friendship carried real social weight. A servant in a household was told what to do and not why, and 'a servant does not understand what his master is doing,' verse 15. To be told the master's mind was to be treated as a confidant. The ancient world also prized the ideal of a friend who would die for another, as Paul notes in Romans 5:7. Jesus takes that ideal and says it is what He is about to do.

The hostility described in verses 18 to 25 was real for the readers of the Gospel. Jesus had already warned that they would be put out of the synagogues, John 16:2, and that anyone who killed them would think it a service to God. By the time the Gospel was written, membership in the synagogue and loyalty to Jesus had come into conflict for many believers. The sentence 'they hated Me without reason' is therefore a word of comfort that tells them their suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned them but that they share the experience of their Lord.
context.canonical:
Israel as God's vine is one of the Old Testament's most developed images. Psalm 80:8 to 16 recalls how God uprooted a vine from Egypt, drove out the nations and planted it, and then asks why its walls have been broken and it has been burned. Isaiah 5:1 to 7 is the song of the vineyard that yielded sour fruit, and it ends with the explanation, 'the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel.' Jeremiah 2:21 and Hosea 10:1 lament that a choice vine turned wild and fruit went to idols. And Isaiah 27:2 to 6 promises a day when the vineyard will be fruitful again and Israel will 'fill the whole world with fruit.'

The Synoptic Gospels use the same background. In the parable of the tenants, Mark 12:1 to 9, the owner sends servants and finally a beloved son to collect the fruit, and the tenants kill the son. In Luke 13:6 to 9 a fig tree gets one more year before it is cut down. John the Baptist and Jesus both say that the tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, Matthew 3:10 and 7:19. John 15 gathers these threads: the Father seeks fruit, and the Son is the vine that finally yields it.

The rest of the New Testament takes up the teaching about union and fruit. Paul speaks of being 'united with Him' in Romans 6:5 and of branches grafted into an olive tree in Romans 11:17 to 24, where he also warns that those who do not continue in God's kindness may be cut off. He names the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22 and 23 and prays that believers will bear fruit in every good work, Colossians 1:10. John's first letter echoes the hatred of the world, 1 John 3:13, and 1 Peter 4:14 says that the Spirit of glory rests on those who are insulted for Christ's name. The title 'friend of God' belongs to Abraham, Isaiah 41:8, 2 Chronicles 20:7 and James 2:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to see that Christian life is not a program of effort but a life drawn from another. The single point that the whole image presses is dependence: apart from Him, they can do nothing. This was needed by a community that was under pressure and tempted to think that survival depended on its own strength, its own loyalty and its own cleverness.

He also wants them to see that fruit and love are inseparable. The fruit is not mainly results in the world but a life that looks like Jesus, one in which His joy is present, His commandments are kept and His love is shown to others. The question for the reader is not 'how much have I done?' but 'am I remaining in Him?'

The final section is written to prepare the readers for rejection. The author does not hide the cost of belonging to Jesus, and he shows that the hatred of the world is not a sign of failure but a continuation of what was done to the Master. In the midst of that, the church is promised the Spirit and given the job of witness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vine, the branches and the gardener are an illustration and not a set of instructions. Jesus uses them to describe what is true of those who are joined to Him. The commands in the chapter are few and clear: remain in Me, remain in My love, keep My commandments, love one another, bear fruit. The picture explains why these are possible, because the branch does not manufacture life but receives it.

The warnings about branches that are cut off and burned are written to people who are listening to Jesus in the room, and they are meant to drive them to the vine and not into despair. They also do not give a method for judging others. The text speaks of the Father's work, not ours, and the church cannot pick through its members as a gardener picks through branches. And the promise that whatever you ask will be done, verse 7, is tied to remaining in Him and to His words remaining in the believer. It describes a prayer shaped by that life and not an open offer to have anything we want.

debates.question: Who are the branches that bear no fruit and are cut off, verses 2 and 6?

views.label: Those who profess faith but have no real union with Christ
views.case: Jesus says the branches are 'in Me,' yet the test is fruit. Judas has just left the room, John 13:30, and is the nearest example of one who was close to Jesus without being joined to Him. On this view the fruitless branch was never a living part of the vine, and 1 John 2:19 describes a similar pattern, of people who went out from the church and showed by leaving that they had not belonged.

views.label: Genuine believers who can fall away
views.case: Another tradition holds that the branch is truly in Christ and may be cut off if it does not remain, as the warnings of Romans 11:22 and Hebrews 6 suggest. The command to remain, repeated so often, is read as a real condition, and verse 6 as a real danger.

views.label: Believers who are lifted up and cared for
views.case: The Greek verb airo in verse 2 means both 'take away' and 'lift up.' Some argue that a vinedresser lifts a trailing branch off the ground to give it light and air, so that the verse describes the Father's care of struggling believers. Most commentators hold that 'take away' is the more natural sense, since verse 6 speaks of the branch being thrown away and burned.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is taken, the practical message is the same. Union with Christ is the only source of life, remaining in Him is the way to live, and the warning is a call to hold on to Him and not to trust in outward association.

debates.question: What is the fruit?

views.label: Christlike character
views.case: Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness and the rest, Galatians 5:22 and 23, and John's chapter itself speaks of love and joy, verses 9 to 12. Fruit is what a life joined to Christ naturally produces.

views.label: New disciples and the spread of the gospel
views.case: In John 12:24 the grain of wheat that dies bears 'much fruit,' meaning a harvest of people, and verse 16 speaks of going to bear fruit that will remain. On this view fruit is converts who come to Christ through the disciples' witness, and the witness of verse 27 is part of it.

views.label: Answered prayer and obedience
views.case: Verses 7 and 16 link fruit with asking and receiving, and verse 10 with keeping commandments. Fruit would then include the whole life of obedience and prayer that flows from the union.

debates.bearing: The chapter does not force a choice. A life joined to Jesus is marked by His character, shows itself in love, and draws others to Him. Fruit is the whole life that comes from the vine.

debates.question: Is friendship with Jesus conditional on obedience, verse 14?

views.label: Obedience is the evidence, not the price
views.case: Jesus has already said that He chose them and laid down His life for them, verses 13 and 16. The love comes first, and obedience is the response. 'You are My friends if you do what I command' describes who His friends are, not how to earn the title.

views.label: Obedience is a real condition for remaining in His love
views.case: Verse 10 says, 'If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love,' and the pattern is set by Jesus who kept the Father's commands. On this view a friendship that ignores His word has already been broken.

debates.bearing: Both readings guard the same truth. The initiative is always His, and the love He gives shapes a life of obedience that is not a burden but the way a friend responds to a friend.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'true' in 'the true vine' is alethinos. It does not mean the opposite of false but something real, genuine, the original of which others are copies. John uses it of the 'true Light' in 1:9 and the 'true bread' in 6:32. The Old Testament pictured Israel as God's vine, and Jesus now claims to be the vine in the full sense, the one in whom the image reaches its goal. The Father is the georgos, the farmer or vinedresser, the one who works the ground, which the BSB renders as 'keeper of the vineyard.'

Verse 2 offers two verbs that turn on one word. The first is airo, which commonly means 'take away' and also means 'lift up,' and translators disagree about which sense fits the fruitless branch. The second is kathairo, 'prune' or 'cleanse,' and in verse 3 the adjective katharos, 'clean,' comes from the same root. Jesus is saying that the pruning of the Father has already been done to them by His word. In John 13:10 the same adjective was used of the disciples after the foot washing.

The verb meno, 'remain' or 'abide,' is the heart of the chapter. It is a verb of staying put, lasting and dwelling, and John uses it in the Gospel for the Spirit who 'remained' on Jesus in 1:32 and for the believer who feeds on Him in 6:56. Here it is used for the mutual indwelling of Jesus and His people, 'Remain in Me, and I will remain in you,' verse 4. It appears again in the phrase 'fruit that will remain,' verse 16, so the verb binds union and lasting results. The command is a present tense, a continuing action, and not a single act.

Jesus says He no longer calls them servants but friends, doulos and philos, verse 15. The word philos belongs to the family of phileo, a word of warm affection, and is the word used of Abraham, God's friend, in the Greek of Isaiah 41:8. In verse 16 He says 'I chose you, and I appointed you,' using ethēka, a form of tithemi, the verb used in verse 13 for laying down one's life, so the same verb describes what He does for them and the place He gives them. The word 'chose,' eklegomai, is repeated in verse 19.

The statement 'they hated Me without reason' in verse 25 uses dorean, 'freely' or 'without cause,' the word in the Greek version of Psalms 35:19 and 69:4, which John calls 'their Law,' a wide use of the word for the Scriptures. In verse 26 the Spirit 'proceeds from the Father,' ekporeuetai. The verb has been central to later debates over the Spirit's origin, but in this verse it describes the Spirit's mission as coming from the Father, and the Son is the one who sends. The word for 'testify,' martureo, is the language of the courtroom witness, and it is used of the Spirit and of the disciples alike.

typology.type: Israel as the LORD's vine, Psalm 80:8 to 16 and Isaiah 5:1 to 7
typology.fulfillment: God brought a vine out of Egypt, planted it, cleared the ground and expected good fruit, but Israel yielded sour grapes. Psalm 80 ends with a prayer for 'the root Your right hand has planted, the son You have raised up for Yourself,' verse 15, and for 'the son of man You have raised up,' verse 17. Jesus is the vine that finally satisfies the planter, and in Him the people are made fruitful. The correspondence is of a vine that God planted for fruit. The escalation is that the vine is the Son Himself, and that others are joined to Him by life. The type falls short because Israel was a nation of a bloodline, while the new vine is entered by faith.

Ezekiel asks what vine wood is good for, and answers that it is useless for any task and is given to the fire. A branch that is cut from the vine has no value except as fuel. Jesus uses the same logic in verse 6, in which a branch that does not remain is thrown away, gathered and burned. The pattern is that life and usefulness belong only to what is joined to its source. The escalation is that Ezekiel's judgment was on a nation, while Jesus' warning is addressed to each person. The type falls short because Ezekiel gave no way back, while the invitation of verse 4 is to remain and to come in.

typology.type: Abraham and Moses as friends of God, Isaiah 41:8 and Exodus 33:11
typology.fulfillment: Abraham is called God's friend in Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7, and the LORD spoke with Moses 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend,' Exodus 33:11. These friendships were rare and marked out a few. Jesus tells all His disciples that they are now friends, because He has made known to them everything He has learned from the Father. The correspondence is the share in God's counsel. The escalation is that the friendship is opened to the whole community and secured by Christ's death. The type falls short in that Abraham and Moses were friends by faith and favour, while the disciples are friends by the laying down of a life.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer who is hated without cause, Psalm 69:4 and 35:19
typology.fulfillment: David cried that those who hate him without cause outnumber the hairs of his head, and that his enemies gloat over him for no reason. Jesus applies this to Himself in verse 25 and says that the world's hatred of Him was foretold. The correspondence is of an innocent man hated by those who ought to have been his own people. The escalation is that Jesus is not only wronged but sinless, and His rejection is the rejection of the Father, verse 23. The type falls short because David was a sinner who also suffered justly for his own sins at times, while Jesus suffers entirely without cause.

study.christ:
Christ is presented as the one in whom God's purpose for His people is at last achieved. The Old Testament vine was planted, tended and pruned, and yielded sour fruit. Jesus is the vine that yields what the Father wants, and He does it as the one who has kept His Father's commandments and remains in His love, verse 10. He does not only say that He is the source of life for believers; He says that He has lived the life that bears fruit, and invites them into it.

He is also the source without whom nothing can be done. 'Apart from Me you can do nothing,' verse 5, is a claim that would be absurd from anyone but God. John 1:3 says that without Him nothing was made, and here he says that without Him nothing that matters in the new life is done. The believer does not borrow a little power from Christ for a few tasks. The whole of the fruitful life flows from union with Him, which is what Paul means when he writes of being united with Him in His death and resurrection, Romans 6:5.

He is the friend who lays down His life. 'Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends,' verse 13, is a statement of what He is about to do, and the next verses show that the love does not stop at the cross but extends into knowledge. He tells them what the Father has told Him. He opens the household of God to them as friends and not servants. And He says that the choice was His, verse 16, so that their security rests on His grip on them and not on theirs on Him.

He is the one the world hated. The statement 'it hated Me first,' verse 18, places Him at the head of the line of the persecuted. The disciples are not walking into something He has not already suffered. Hating Him is hating the Father, verse 23, which makes plain that He is not a mere messenger. And He is the sender of the Spirit, 'whom I will send to you from the Father,' verse 26, who will testify about Him. The Son who goes to the cross is the Son who gives the Spirit.

A word of care is needed. The image of the vine is not a coded allegory of every detail, and nothing is gained by asking who the pruning knife is. The links to Christ rest on His own words, 'I am the true vine,' on the Old Testament pattern of Israel as God's vine, and on the New Testament's language of union with Him, as in Galatians 2:20 and Ephesians 3:17.
study.god:
The Father is the gardener, and the picture of Him is surprising in its tenderness. He is not distant. He works the vineyard, watches each branch, lifts, cuts and cleans, and He does it for a reason: that the branches may bear more fruit and that He may be glorified, verse 8. God's glory in this chapter is not served by display but by the fruitfulness of His people. Hosea 14:8 says it in another way: 'your fruit comes from Me.' The fruit is the Father's gift through the Son.

God is shown as a God who loves within the Trinity and shares that love outward. 'As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you,' verse 9, sets a chain in motion, from Father to Son to disciples. Jesus then says that He keeps the Father's commandments and remains in His love, verse 10, and invites them to remain in His. The love that flows among the persons of God is not closed in on itself but opens to include a company of friends. The prayer of John 17:21 to 23 speaks of the same union, 'May they also be in Us.'

The chapter keeps the Father's action and the believer's responsibility together. The Father prunes and cuts off, Jesus chooses and appoints, and believers are told to remain, keep and love. The tension is not resolved by reducing one side. The vine is the Lord's, and the life is His, yet the branch is addressed as a responsible person who is told to stay. This is the pattern of grace in the whole Bible, in which God's initiative does not remove human response but makes it possible.

The Spirit appears as the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father and testifies about the Son, verse 26. The Father sends Him in the Son's name, as in 14:26, and the Son sends Him from the Father here. The persons are distinct and share one work. Eastern and Western churches have long argued over the precise relation of the Spirit's procession to the Son, but this text states what all share, that the Spirit comes from the Father and that Jesus sends Him.

For worship the image gives a plain shape. God is honoured when His people are fruitful, and the way to honour Him is to remain, to stay in His word, His love and His commands. The worship of the church is not only singing but a life drawn from the vine and bearing fruit to His glory, and the joy that results, Jesus says, is His own joy in them, made complete, verse 11.

crossReferences.note: The song of the vineyard that produced sour fruit, ending with the identification, 'the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel.' It is the background of the claim to be the true vine. Where the first vineyard yielded bloodshed and cries of distress, the true vine yields the fruit God had looked for.

The psalm remembers how God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it, and now asks Him to look down and attend to it. The prayer for the son He raised up for Himself finds an answer in Jesus, the Son who is also the vine. It shows how the image of vine and Son were already linked in Israel's prayers.

A promise that in the day to come, God Himself will guard a fruitful vineyard and Israel will 'fill the whole world with fruit.' The promise is larger than the nation and hints at the nations being reached. In John 15 the world is filled with fruit through the branches that remain in Christ.

The prophet's question, what is the wood of a vine good for, and the answer, the fire. It stands behind verse 6, in which the branch that does not remain is gathered and burned. It shows that the point is not the worth of the branch in itself but of the life that it receives.

The parable of the vineyard and its tenants. The owner sends servants and then his beloved son, and the tenants kill the son. It helps explain the chapter's two moods: the Father looks for fruit, and the world hates the Son who comes. John 15:18 to 25 is the experience behind the parable.

Paul's list of the fruit of the Spirit. Love, joy and peace stand first, as in John 15:9 to 12, where Jesus speaks of love and a joy made complete. It shows that fruit is a quality of life and not a task, and that the Spirit is the one who produces it in the believer.

The olive tree gives another picture of union. Branches are broken off and others grafted in, and the grafted are warned to continue in God's kindness. It runs alongside John 15 and shows that Paul, too, spoke of belonging to God's people as being joined to a living root, and that he also pressed the need to continue.

Abraham believed God, and 'he was called a friend of God.' The title is set in the Old Testament, Isaiah 41:8, and James quotes it to show that faith and a life of obedience belong together. It shows that Jesus' words to His disciples confer on all of them a title once held by a few.

David's cry about those who hate him without cause. Jesus quotes the substance of it in verse 25 as part of 'their Law,' using the Psalter as Scripture that speaks of Himself. It shows that His rejection did not take God by surprise and was already written into the story of the righteous sufferer.

Jesus prays that His people may be one, as the Father and the Son are one, and may be in Them. It is the prayer form of the vine discourse: union with the Son is union with the Father, and its fruit is a unity that persuades the world. The vine and the prayer interpret each other.

'Do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.' John's later letter repeats the teaching of verse 18, to a church that was suffering for the same reason. It shows how the message of the upper room was handed on to believers in the next generation, who needed to hear that opposition is not a sign that they have gone astray.

study.oneStory:
God's purpose from the beginning was a fruitful people. Adam and Eve were told to be fruitful and fill the earth, and Abraham was promised descendants and a blessing for all nations. The vine of Israel was planted to carry that blessing, and the prophets mourned that it produced bad fruit. The question that hangs over the Old Testament is whether any branch will finally bear what God planted it to bear.

John 15 answers that God has found a vine that does not fail. Jesus is the true Israel, the faithful son who keeps the Father's commandments and remains in His love, and He is also the vine into which others are grafted. The fruit God wanted from Israel is produced in those who are joined to Him. In this way the story of the vineyard finds its resolution without being abandoned. The people of God are renewed from inside by the life of the Son.

The chapter also explains the shape of the church's life in the time between the cross and the return. The disciples will be hated, as their Master was, and they will also be given the Spirit who testifies. Mission and suffering are bound together. Witness to the world is carried out by people who are loved, chosen and joined to Him, and who bear fruit that lasts.

The story does not end with the vine. It ends with a tree of life beside the river in the new creation, Revelation 22:2, with leaves for the healing of the nations, and with a company of friends who live in the presence of the One who laid down His life for them. The branches that remained in Him then see what the fruit was for. The Father who tended the vineyard gathers the harvest, and the Son's joy, which He promised would be in them, is complete.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by I am the true vine and you are the branches?

options.text: Fruitful life flows only from union with Him; apart from Him the branches can do nothing.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 tie all fruit to remaining in Christ the vine.

options.text: Believers can bear fruit on their own if they try hard enough.
options.note: Jesus says apart from Him you can do nothing; fruit comes only from union with Him.

options.text: It mainly teaches that we should stay busy for God.
options.note: It does call for fruitfulness, but the point is dependent union with Christ, not mere busyness.

options.text: Believers depend on Christ to be fruitful.
options.note: True, but it understates the total dependence, that apart from Him they can do nothing at all.

quiz.q: What is the repeated command at the heart of the vine imagery?

options.text: Remain, or abide, in Christ and in His love.
options.note: The word remain runs through verses 4 to 10 as the key to fruitfulness.

options.text: Work harder to produce fruit by effort.
options.note: Fruitfulness involves real obedience, but the command is to remain in Christ, from whom the fruit flows, not self-powered effort.

options.text: Separate from Christ to prove one's independence.
options.note: The opposite; separation from the vine means withering.

options.text: Stay closely connected to Jesus.
options.note: True, but it does not capture the rich sense of abiding in His love by keeping His word.

quiz.q: How does Jesus describe the greatest love?

options.text: To lay down one's life for one's friends, as He was about to do.
options.note: Verse 13 defines the greatest love, which Jesus embodies at the cross.

options.text: To feel strong affection for many people.
options.note: Affection has a place, but the greatest love Jesus names is the sacrificial act of laying down one's life.

options.text: To keep religious rules carefully.
options.note: The measure of love is self-sacrifice, not rule-keeping.

options.text: To love others sacrificially at real cost.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific and highest form, laying down one's life for one's friends.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say about how the disciples came to be His?

options.text: You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you to bear lasting fruit.
options.note: Verse 16 grounds their standing in Christ's choosing, not their own.

options.text: They responded in faith when Jesus called them.
options.note: Their faith was real, but Jesus stresses the prior truth, you did not choose Me, I chose you.

options.text: They chose Jesus after weighing the options.
options.note: The verse explicitly reverses this: I chose you.

options.text: Jesus chose them to go and bear fruit.
options.note: True, but it omits the pointed contrast, you did not choose Me, and the lasting nature of the fruit.

quiz.q: What does Jesus tell the disciples to expect from the world?

options.text: The world will hate them, because it hated Him first.
options.note: Verses 18 and 19 warn that the world's hatred of Christ falls on His followers.

options.text: The world will welcome and honor them.
options.note: He warns of hatred, not welcome, from the world.

options.text: The world will merely tolerate them at a distance.
options.note: It is not indifference; Jesus warns of active hatred, as the world hated Him first.

options.text: They may face persecution for His name.
options.note: True, but it softens the direct statement that the world will hate them as it hated Him.

questions: Jesus says apart from Him you can do nothing. Where are you trying to bear fruit by your own effort rather than by remaining in Him?
The Father prunes fruitful branches to make them more fruitful. How might a painful season in your life be His loving pruning rather than rejection?
Jesus calls His disciples friends, not servants. How does it change your walk with Him to know you are counted His friend?
You did not choose Me, but I chose you. How does resting in Christ's choosing of you steady your assurance and free you to serve?
Jesus warned that the world would hate His followers as it hated Him. Where are you tempted to soften your allegiance to Christ to avoid the world's disapproval?

translationNotes.note: I am the true vine draws on Isaiah 5 and Psalm 80, where Israel is God's vine; Jesus presents Himself as the true vine that bears the fruit Israel did not.
No servant is greater than his master recalls John 13:16; because Jesus was persecuted, His servants will be too.
They hated Me without reason fulfills the psalms of the righteous sufferer; the BSB footnote points to Psalms 35:19, 38:19, and 69:4.
Advocate renders parakletos; the BSB footnote gives Comforter, Helper, or Counselor. The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father and testifies about the Son.
